verdicts.trueWording: As the reader experiences the story, he drags that same baggage through the reading.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200) carries the quote word for word. Full context: characters 'acquire baggage' when hurt physically or emotionally, and the reader drags that same baggage through the reading. Both limbs (reader; character's accumulated baggage) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I often had to trust that the reader would make a leap and connect events even if Fitz was not seeing the connection.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the raw page. The 'leap the narrator did not make' limb is explicit: 'even if Fitz was not seeing the connection' — Fitz is the first-person narrator, and the answer is the first-person-limits question.

verdicts.trueWording: In Farseer, I coped with that by having little prologues at the beginning of each chapter that gave the reader additional information.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Every limb supported: coping with first-person limitation ('the writer is limited to telling the reader what that character knows at that moment'), in Farseer, chapter-opening prologues, additional information.

verdicts.trueWording: There is a fairly clean dividing line between the Robin Hobb voice and the Megan Lindholm voice in my writing.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the first interview excerpt on the raw Locus Online page (December 2005 issue thread). Claim's 'in her writing' is the page's 'in my writing'.

verdicts.trueWording: I would describe my writing style as both leisurely and intimate.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, first Q&A of the Fantasy Book Critic interview (post dated Monday, January 7, 2008).

verdicts.trueWording: For me, that means putting in details and incidents that may not directly move the plot forward.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the characterization answer; the antecedent of 'that' is 'the key to strong characterization is taking the time to develop the character', so the 'characterisation means' limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: The pacing at the beginning of any of my books is usually a lot slower than towards the end of the book.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the claim's completion ('a lot slower than towards the end') is the page's own continuation of the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: simply because so many words are given over to character construction
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and it is the causal clause attached directly to the slow-opening sentence ('The pacing at the beginning ... is usually a lot slower ..., simply because ...'), so the attribution limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: That seems more like a joke than a devastating occurrence.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The illustration on the page is exactly two sentences — 'Joe had been Ed's best friend since childhood. One night Joe got drunk and accidentally ran over Ed.' — a friend killing a friend, offered as what happens without earned build-up.

verdicts.trueWording: when I propelled the reader directly into it, it lacked the impact and significance I wanted it to have
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The 'without building up to it' limb is the preceding clause on the page: 'when I didn't slow down and construct the ramps up to that exciting scene'.

verdicts.trueWording: For me, the story is really about how the events affect the characters rather than about the events themselves.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 1 of the Pat's Fantasy Hotlist Q&A (posted Monday, July 11, 2005).

verdicts.trueWording: With every sentence, you narrow an infinite number of possibilities down to a single track.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 2; the 'down to a single track' limb is the page's own sentence ending.

verdicts.trueWording: Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the fan transcript of Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (page header names the episode and links writingexcuses.com/2016/10/12). Spoken by [Robin]; the differentiation limb holds — the passage answers how to tell two similar characters apart and continues 'There's just a lot of ways to build that in.'

verdicts.trueWording: So with your characters, it's a choice of vocabulary, it's a way of seeing things.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, attributed to [Robin] in the same transcript, and framed as how to differentiate characters (followed by the read-your-dialogue double-check).

verdicts.trueWording: I'm married to a sailor. In our house, we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck. I happen to have like a kitchen and a bathroom and a floor.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. All limbs supported: her own household, occupational vocabulary (farmer vs sailing-ship background), and the same rooms under two names — the page adds 'But it's all in the same house.'
